newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan war refugees come home to peace.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan war refugees come home to peace.

text.p: The first wave of refugees returning to Guatemala in peacetime crossed the border from Mexico on Friday, saying it was the promise of free land that drew them.

"We're happy to return to our country," 18-year-old Marselino Torres, a Chuj descendant of the Maya Indians, told Reuters, gazing with fascination out of the bus window as he crossed through this frontier town.
"Our familes who stayed in Mexico are sad but we returned for a piece of land," he said.

He and his young wife Juana Carmela were among 129 families, making a total of 499 refugees, who came home in the first mass return since a Dec. 29 peace accord ended Guatemala's 36-year armed rebellion, the longest and bloodiest in Central America.
The conflict uprooted hundreds of thousands -- mainly Indian peasants from the western highlands -- and left an estimated 100,000 dead and 40,000 disappeared.

The couple, who met and wed in a refugee camp in the southern Mexican state of Chiapas, were returning to a homeland they had never entered, where social tensions still persist especially in the remote and underdeveloped northeast where they will settle.

But the area awaiting the returning convoy is a 2,500-acre (990-hectare) plantation, purchased by the government for $1.5 million, coming with fields of coffee and cardamom and 200 head of cattle that will be divided up between them.
"We liked it in Mexico but there we had no land," said 80-year-old Manuel Hernandez Calvo.
More than 30,000 registered refugees remained in Mexican camps in Chiapas and the Yucatan. About 19,000 have come home in organised returns that began in 1993.
Ironically, peacetime Guatemala had seen a halt in the return process until now.
"We thought this government would make the returns go faster. It turned out the opposite," said Rafael Figueroa of the non-government Permenant Commissions of Guatemala Refugees in Mexico.

Last year's peace negotiations and a four-month guerrilla demobilization this year were priorities for the administratrion of President Alvaro Arzu, Figueroa said, delaying the purchase of land for refugees.
